newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik refugees return home after civil war.
newsitem.headline: Tajik refugees return home after civil war.

text.p: The first group of Tajik refugees returned from Afghanistan to their war-scarred homeland, expressing confidence in a peace deal between the government and its Islamic opponents.
Many of the 250 returnees kissed the arid mountain ground as they stepped from a rusty, overcrowded barge which ferried them from the Afghan shore across the rushing Pyandzh river on Thursday.
"Now we wish Tajikistan to live in peace and we are glad to have returned to our motherland," said Madzhida, 48. "Five years ago we fled from one war but got into another one," she said.
Haggard and dressed in tatters, many returnees exuded hope for a new life in the former Soviet republic they left in 1992-93 at the height of a bitter civil war.

In exile, many were caught up in the endless fighting of Afghanistan. Despite an accord signed in Moscow last month, Tajikistan's peace remains exposed to violence from maverick armed bands at large in the rugged country of 5.7 million.
Many refugees, some of whom brought cars, cows and other animals with them, carried planks taken from their temporary shelters in exile to be used in building new houses back home.

The crossing point at Nizhny Pyandzh, some 200 km (125 miles) south of the Tajik capital Dushanbe, is one of two selected by the Tajik government for the return of some 20,000 Tajiks still in exile across the former Soviet frontier in Afghanistan.

Around 60,000 Tajiks fled but about 40,000 refugees have already returned since late 1994, when Tajikistan's secular Moscow-backed government started negotiations with the Islamic opposition, some of whose forces had operated from Afghan soil.
Much of Afghanistan is now controlled by the fundamentalist Islamic Taleban militia and many young Tajik women were clad in black tunics or burkas, revealing only their eyes.

"This is our motherland, and this is why we decided to return," said Gulchekhra, 17, her body swathed in black, with a black yashmak hiding her face. She left Tajikistan five years ago, together with her family, because of the civil war.
On June 27 in Moscow, the government and opposition agreed a final peace deal deal which ended the war that had killed tens of thousands and left many more living as refugees.
"We attach great importance to this repatriation, because it is the first since the peace deal," said Gang Li, head of the Tajik mission of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).

"Now the process of repatriation depends on the political situation in Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and we plan to complete it within three months," Nigmatullo Abdullolov, opposition member of the Tajik refugee commission, told Reuters.

The returnees -- treated to Tajik potato-and-rice soup known as mastova --- spent Friday at a makeshift camp near the village of Nizhny Pyandzh before being taken by bus to their homes in the Kurgan Tyube region of southern Tajikistan.
They face severe financial difficulties but have been promised assistance.
"We want to help them rebuild their lives by developing small enterprises in their villages," said UNHCR's Li.
